opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's something we thought about a lot. Our general philosophy was that you shouldn't over-optimize for the benchmark itself. What we actually care about is whether the model is good at real software engineering, and SWE-bench is just a proxy for that.

There's a real tension, though. Some prompt changes help on the easier problems, where the model mostly needs to find the right file and make a small, clean edit. Other changes help on the harder problems, where the model has to explore the codebase more, form hypotheses, write a reproduction script, and iterate. Those can pull in different directions. If you push the model to be more thorough and careful, you sometimes lose a bit on the easy cases because it overthinks or makes unnecessary changes. If you push it to be fast and decisive, it does worse on the hard ones.

I put more weight on the hard problems, for a couple of reasons. First, the easy ones are increasingly saturated. Most reasonable setups get them, so they don't tell you much. The hard problems are where you see real differences in capability and where the next gains come from. Second, the hard problems look more like what engineers actually want help with. Nobody needs an agent for a one-line fix they could do in thirty seconds. The value is in the messy, multi-file, "I don't even know where the bug is" problems.

That said, I wouldn't adopt a prompt that crushed the hard problems but regressed a lot overall. That usually means you've introduced some weird behavior. What you really want is a prompt that gives the model good general habits: understand the problem, reproduce it, fix it, verify the fix. That kind of prompt tends to hold up across difficulty levels instead of being tuned to one slice. And honestly, much of our work was keeping the scaffolding simple and letting the model do the work, rather than writing very specific prompt instructions that might overfit to one subset of the benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges tradeoffs and favors prompts with general habits that work across difficulty levels, explicitly cautioning against tuning to one benchmark subset. This communicates that the distinction should not be obsessively optimized, even though it gives hard problems greater weight.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and honestly I think it matters more than people give it credit for. When we were building out the SWE-bench agent, one thing we noticed pretty quickly is that a lot of prompt changes would move the overall number by a couple of points, but when you actually looked at where the gains were coming from, it was almost entirely the easy and medium problems. You'd get a model that was a little more consistent on the stuff it could already basically do, and the hard tail would just sit there unchanged.

And I think that's a trap, because the easy problems are the ones that are going to get saturated anyway. Every model release is going to pick those up. The hard problems are where you actually learn something about what the model is bad at. So when I'm looking at a prompt or a scaffold change, I care a lot about the split. If something moves the hard bucket, even if the overall score is flat or slightly down, that's usually telling me something real about the model's reasoning or its ability to explore the codebase, and that's the thing I want to double down on.

The flip side is that the hard bucket is small and noisy. You can fool yourself really easily. A three-problem swing on hard SWE-bench looks like a big percentage change and might be entirely noise from the model taking a slightly different path. So we tried to run multiple samples and look at pass rates per problem rather than just the aggregate. If a change is consistently flipping the same handful of hard problems from fail to pass, that's a signal. If it's just reshuffling which hard problems happen to pass this run, that's not.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the prompts that helped on the overall number were things like being more conservative, like telling the model to make smaller edits or to stop earlier. And that's kind of the opposite of what you want on the hard problems, where the model actually needs to go investigate, run tests, dig around in files it wasn't pointed at. So there was a real tension there. Our philosophy ended up being pretty minimal, give the model good tools and get out of its way, because the heavy-handed prompting that boosts the easy stuff tends to cap the ceiling on the hard stuff. And the ceiling is what we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the distinction matters more than people give it credit for, emphasizes caring about the split, and prioritizes gains on hard problems. It does not judge the distinction as unworthy of attention.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters quite a bit, because the overall score can hide where a prompt is helping. You might have a prompt that makes the model more persistent, which helps on a hard problem, but on an easy problem it just overthinks things and makes unnecessary changes.

So I’d want to look at both: does this improve performance overall, and what happens as the problems get harder? Ideally, you want the model to adapt—to do the straightforward thing when that’s enough, and spend more effort when it actually needs to. A prompt that wins on the hardest subset is useful evidence, but it’s not automatically the best default.

r001.rationale: The response says the distinction matters “quite a bit” and recommends examining both overall performance and performance as problems get harder, contradicting the criterion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction matters quite a bit, because an overall score can hide where the improvement is coming from. A prompt might help the model solve more straightforward issues while doing very little for the harder ones. And another prompt might help it stick with a difficult problem, but add unnecessary complexity on easy tasks.

So I’d want to look at both: does it improve performance overall, and does it actually move the frontier of what the model can solve? You also have to be careful with the hard subset, because there are fewer examples and it’s easier to overfit to a handful of results. Ultimately, I’d put the most weight on improvements that hold up across problems you haven’t been tuning against.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the distinction “matters quite a bit” and recommends evaluating both overall and hard-subset performance, contradicting the criterion that it is not worth obsessing over.
